pending_part_2.voiceover_script: In Part 1, we explored the massive 1997 acoustic anomaly known as The Bloop, but when oceanographers finally cracked the data, the explanation was far more unsettling. Years later, NOAA scientists deployed high-grade hydrophones directly into the remote sector of the southern Pacific Ocean and discovered a cataclysmic geological event. The Bloop wasn't made by a colossal, undiscovered sea monster lurking in the abyss. It was the distinct, booming signature of ice calving—a massive Antarctic glacier fracturing and breaking apart under immense pressure. Yet, despite the official ice-quake conclusion, sonar logs from that exact coordinate still contain a bizarre secondary audio frequency that experts have never been able to publicly explain. Was it really just cracking ice, or did something down there answer back?
